# Definition

:::{.definition data-title="Transport Equation"}

The **transport equation** is a **first-order**
[[partial-differential-equations|PDE]] that describes how a quantity is carried
along by a flow without being created or destroyed. In its simplest form, with
constant velocity $c\in\mathbb{R}^n$, the transport equation with initial data
$u_0$ is given by
$$
\begin{cases}
\partial_t u + c\cdot \nabla u = 0, & t>0,\ x\in\mathbb{R}^n, \\
u(0,x) = u_0(x).
\end{cases}
$$

:::

In one space dimension this reads $u_t+cu_x=0$.

## Derivative Along a Vector

:::{.definition data-title="Derivative along a vector"}

Let $\vec V$ be a vector and $u=u(x)$ a differentiable function of
$x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)$. The **derivative of $u$ along $\vec V$** is
$$
\partial_{\vec V}u \coloneqq \nabla u \cdot \vec V = \sum_{i=1}^n V_i\,\partial_{x_i} u.
$$

:::

The transport equation is therefore the statement that $u$ has zero derivative
along the space-time vector $(1,c)$, i.e. $\partial_{(1,c)}u=0$ for
$u=u(t,x)$. See [[gradient#Directional Derivative|directional derivative]].

# Solution

:::{.theorem data-title="Solution of the Transport Equation"}

If $u_0\in C^1$, the unique $C^1$ solution of the transport equation is
$$
u(t,x)=u_0(x-ct).
$$

:::

:::{.proof}

Fix $x_0$ and consider the line $x(s)=x_0+cs$ in space. By the
[[chain-rule|chain rule]]
$$
\frac{d}{ds}u(s,x(s))=u_t+c\cdot\nabla u=0,
$$
so $u$ is constant along the line, hence $u(t,x_0+ct)=u(0,x_0)=u_0(x_0)$. Every
point $(t,x)$ lies on exactly one such line, namely the one through
$x_0=x-ct$, which gives $u(t,x)=u_0(x-ct)$ and shows uniqueness. Conversely
this function satisfies the equation by the chain rule.

:::

The lines $x=x_0+ct$ are the **characteristics** of the PDE (see
[[method-of-characteristics]]). The solution is the initial profile translated
at speed $c$ without changing shape. In the $(x,t)$ plane these are parallel
lines of slope $1/c$, and the value of $u$ at a point is read off by following
the characteristic back to $t=0$.

:::{.example}

**Rescaled equation.** For $a\,u_t+b\,u_x=0$ with $a\neq0$ divide by $a$ to get
speed $c=b/a$, so $u(t,x)=u_0\!\left(x-\tfrac{b}{a}t\right)$. For
$2u_t+3u_x=0$ the characteristics are $x=\tfrac32t+x_0$.

:::

# Generalizations

## Damping and Source Terms

For $u_t+cu_x+\lambda u=f(t,x)$ the PDE becomes an ODE along each
characteristic, with $U(s)=u(s,x_0+cs)$:
$$
U'(s)+\lambda U(s)=f(s,x_0+cs),\qquad U(0)=u_0(x_0).
$$
Solving with the integrating factor $e^{\lambda s}$ and setting $x_0=x-ct$,
$$
u(t,x)=e^{-\lambda t}u_0(x-ct)+\int_0^t e^{-\lambda(t-s)}f\big(s,\,x-c(t-s)\big)\,ds.
$$

In particular, pure decay ($f=0$) gives $u=e^{-\lambda t}u_0(x-ct)$: the profile
translates and its amplitude decays exponentially, and a source ($\lambda=0$)
adds the accumulated contributions along the characteristic.

## Variable Velocity

For $u_t+b(t,x)\cdot\nabla u=0$ the characteristics solve the ODE
$$
\dot x(s)=b(s,x(s)),
$$
and $u$ is constant along each of them. They are no longer straight lines, and
the solution is $u(t,x)=u_0(X_0)$ where $X_0$ is the starting point of the
characteristic passing through $(t,x)$.

## Conservative Form

$$
\partial_t\rho+\nabla\cdot(\rho b)=0
$$
is the continuity equation for a density $\rho$ advected by the field $b$.
Expanding the divergence,
$$
\partial_t\rho+b\cdot\nabla\rho=-\rho\,\nabla\cdot b,
$$
so it differs from the form above when $\nabla\cdot b\neq0$, since the density
can then compress or expand.

## Non-Linear Case

For $u_t+c(u)u_x=0$ the characteristics are still straight lines, with slope
determined by the data,
$$
x=x_0+c(u_0(x_0))\,t,
$$
and $u$ is constant on each, giving the implicit solution
$u=u_0\big(x-c(u)t\big)$. Characteristics can cross, producing shocks, at which
point classical solutions fail and weak solutions and entropy conditions are
needed.

# Derivation From Conservation Laws

Let $u(t,x)$ be the density of a quantity in a medium moving with velocity $V$.
Conservation of mass on an arbitrary region $\Omega$ states that the rate of
change of the amount in $\Omega$ equals minus the flux through $\partial\Omega$:
$$
\frac{d}{dt}\int_\Omega u\,dx=-\int_{\partial\Omega}\vec J\cdot\vec n\,dS
=-\int_\Omega\nabla\cdot\vec J\,dx,
$$
by the divergence theorem. Since $\Omega$ is arbitrary,
$$
u_t+\nabla\cdot\vec J=0.
$$

- **Pure transport:** $\vec J=u\vec V$ gives $u_t+\nabla\cdot(u\vec V)=0$, which
  is $u_t+\vec V\cdot\nabla u=0$ for constant $\vec V$.
- **Transport and diffusion:** adding the diffusion flux $-k\nabla u$ (Fourier's
  law, see [[heat-equation]]) gives $\vec J=u\vec V-k\nabla u$ and so
  $$
  u_t+\vec V\cdot\nabla u=k\,\Delta u
  $$
  for constant $\vec V$.
